title: Chemistry — Mission 5: The Sealed Container
description: A sealed gas canister is due for a safety inspection, and the readings don't match what the manifest predicted. Work through the gas laws before you sign off on it.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Won't sign off on anything until the numbers actually check out.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Assumes gas behavior is basically unpredictable.

gas_laws_sheet.name: Gas Laws Reference Sheet
gas_laws_sheet.description: Boyle's, Charles's, Gay-Lussac's, and the combined/ideal gas laws, all in one place.

pressure_gauge.name: Pressure Gauge
pressure_gauge.description: Reads the canister's current internal pressure.

elements.text: This canister was sealed at room temperature, but it's been sitting near the radiator all week. The manifest pressure doesn't match today's reading.
Gases are just unpredictable, right? Maybe it's fine.

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the gas laws reference sheet.

options.text: "Not unpredictable — if the volume's fixed and temperature rose, the pressure should have risen too. Let's check the numbers."

elements.text: Good, sheet in hand. Let's work through which law actually applies here.
No sheet yet — we can't sign off on a guess. Let's fix that.

config.question: The canister's volume is fixed and only its temperature changed. Which gas law relates pressure and temperature at constant volume?
config.explanation: With volume fixed, pressure and absolute temperature are directly proportional — that's Gay-Lussac's Law.

config.question: Sealed at 20 degrees C and 100 kPa, the canister is now at 40 degrees C with the same volume. Using absolute temperature, what should the new pressure be closest to?

options.text: About 107 kPa — a modest rise from the higher absolute temperature
200 kPa — pressure doubles when Celsius temperature doubles
100 kPa — pressure doesn't depend on temperature
50 kPa — pressure drops as temperature rises

config.explanation: Using Kelvin (293 K to 313 K), P2 = P1 x (T2/T1) = 100 x (313/293) ≈ 107 kPa — a modest rise, not a doubling, because Celsius doesn't scale proportionally but Kelvin does.

config.prompt: Order these steps for solving any gas law problem, first to last.

items.text: Identify which variable is held constant

elements.text: The reading matches the prediction exactly. Safe to sign off — the canister is behaving exactly as the gas laws say it should.
We got there, but next time let's run the numbers before assuming the gauge is wrong.

elements.prompt: The inspection form is ready. What now?

options.text: Walk Dev through why gas behavior is completely predictable once you use Kelvin.
Sign off and move on. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So it's not random at all — it's just a ratio, as long as you remember to use Kelvin instead of Celsius. I was overcomplicating it.

ending.title: Gas Law Inspector
ending.description: Predicted the pressure reading exactly from the gas laws and taught Dev why gases aren't unpredictable.

ending.title: Inspection Signed
ending.description: The canister passed inspection. The deeper gas-law reasoning can wait.
